sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen6788" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="1Kgs.13" sID="1Kgs.13"/> <div eID="gen6788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6789" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6790" type="x-p"/> In the close of the foregoing chapter we left Jeroboam attending his altar at Beth-el, and there we find him in the beginning of this, when he received a testimony from God against his idolatry and apostasy. This was sent to him by a prophet, a man of God that lived in Judah, who is the principal subject of the story of this chapter, where we are told, I. What passed between him and the new king. 1. The prophet threatened Jeroboam's altar (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.1-1Kgs.13.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), and gave him a sign (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.3">ver. 3</reference>), which immediately came to pass, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.5">ver. 5</reference>. 2. The king threatened the prophet, and was himself made another sign, by the withering of his hand (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.4">ver. 4</reference>), and the restoring of it upon his submission and the prophet's intercession, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.6">ver. 6</reference>. 3. The prophet refused the kindness offered him thereupon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.7-1Kgs.13.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. II. What passed between him and the old prophet. 1. The old prophet fetched him back by a lie, and gave him entertainment, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.11-1Kgs.13.19">ver. 11-19</reference>. 2. He, for accepting it, in disobedience to the divine command, is threatened with death, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.20-1Kgs.13.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. And, 3. The threatening is executed, for he is slain by a lion (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.23-1Kgs.13.24">ver. 23, 24</reference>), and buried at Beth-el, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.25-1Kgs.13.32">ver. 25-32</reference>. 4. Jeroboam is hardened in his idolatry, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.33-1Kgs.13.34">ver. 33, 34</reference>. "Thy judgments, Lord, are a great deep."

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 974.)</title> <div sID="gen6791" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And, behold, there came a man of God out of Judah by the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Beth-el: and Jeroboam stood by the altar to burn incense. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he cried against the altar in the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, O altar, altar, thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name; and upon thee shall he offer the priests of the high places that burn incense upon thee, and men's bones shall be burnt upon thee. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he gave a sign the same day, saying, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sign which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken; Behold, the altar shall be rent, and the ashes that <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon it shall be poured out. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it came to pass, when king Jeroboam heard the saying of the man of God, which had cried against the altar in Beth-el, that he put forth his hand from the altar, saying, Lay hold on him. And his hand, which he put forth against him, dried up, so that he could not pull it in again to him. <hi type="super">5</hi> The altar also was rent, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> And the king answered and said unto the man of God, Intreat now the face of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored me again. And the man of God besought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the king's hand was restored him again, and became as <hi type="italic">it was</hi> before. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the king said unto the man of God, Come home with me, and refresh thyself, and I will give thee a reward. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the man of God said unto the king, If thou wilt give me half thine house, I will not go in with thee, neither will I eat bread nor drink water in this place: <hi type="super">9</hi> For so was it charged me by the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest. <hi type="super">10</hi> So he went another way, and returned not by the way that he came to Beth-el. <div eID="gen6791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6792" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A messenger sent to Jeroboam, to signify to him God's displeasure against his idolatry, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.1">v. 1</reference>. The army of Judah that aimed to ruin him was countermanded, and might not draw a sword against him (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.24">ch. xii. 24</reference>); but a prophet of Judah is, instead thereof, sent to reclaim him from his evil way, and is sent in time, while he is but dedicating his altar, before his heart is hardened by the deceitfulness of his sin; for God delights not in the death of sinners, but would rather they would burn and live. How bold was the messenger that durst attack the king in his pride and interrupt the solemnity he was proud of! Those that go on God's errand must not fear the face of man; they know who will bear them out. How kind was he that sent him to warn Jeroboam of the wrath of God <hi type="italic">revealed from heaven</hi> against his <hi type="italic">ungodliness</hi> and <hi type="italic">unrighteousness!</hi> <div eID="gen6792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> II. The message delivered in God's name, not whispered, but cried with a loud voice, denoting both the prophet's courage, that he was neither afraid nor ashamed to own it, and his earnestness, that he desired to be heard and heeded by all that were present, who were not a few, on this great occasion. It was directed, not to Jeroboam nor to the people, but to the altar, the stones of which would sooner hear and yield than those who were mad upon their idols and deaf to divine calls. Yet, in threatening the altar, God threatened the founder and worshippers, to whom it was as dear as their own souls, and who might conclude, "If God's wrath fasten upon the lifeless guiltless altar, how shall we escape?" That which was foretold concerning the altar (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">v. 2</reference>) was that, in process of time, a prince of the house of David, Josiah by name, should pollute this altar by sacrificing the idolatrous priests themselves upon it, and burning the bones of dead men. Let Jeroboam know and be sure, 1. That the altar he now consecrated should be desecrated. Idolatrous worship will not continue, but the word of the Lord will endure for ever. 2. That the <hi type="italic">priests of the high places</hi> he now made should themselves be made sacrifices to the justice of God, and the first and only sacrifices upon this altar that would be pleasing to him. If the offering be such as is an abomination to God, it will follow, of course, that the offerers must themselves fall under his wrath, which will abide upon them, since it is not otherwise transmitted. 3. That this should be done by a branch <hi type="italic">of the house of David.</hi> That family which he and his kingdom had despised and treacherously deserted should recover so much power as to demolish that altar which he thought to establish; so that right and truth should at length prevail, both in civil and sacred matters, notwithstanding the present triumphs of those that were given to change the fear both <hi type="italic">of God and the king.</hi> It was about 356 years ere this prediction was fulfilled, yet it was spoken of as sure and nigh at hand, for a thousand years with God are but as one day. Nothing more contingent and arbitrary than the giving of names to persons, yet Josiah was here named above 300 years before he was born. Nothing future is hidden from God. There are <hi type="italic">names in the book</hi> of the divine prescience (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">Phil. iv. 3</reference>), names <hi type="italic">written in heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> III. A sign is given for the confirming of the truth of this prediction, that the altar should be shaken to pieces by an invisible power and the ashes of the sacrifice scattered (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.3">v. 3</reference>), which came to pass immediately, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.5">v. 5</reference>. This was, 1. A proof that the prophet was sent of God, <hi type="italic">who confirmed the word with this sign following,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.16.20">Mark xvi. 20</reference>. 2. A present indication of God's displeasure against these idolatrous sacrifices. How could the gift be acceptable when the altar that should sanctify it was an abomination? 3. It was a reproach to the people, whose hearts were harder than these stones and rent not under the word of the Lord. 4. It was a specimen of what should be done to it in the accomplishment of this prophecy by Josiah; it was now rent, in token of its being then ruined. <div eID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6795" type="x-p"/> IV. Jeroboam's hand withered, which he stretched out to seize or smite the man of God, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.4">v. 4</reference>. Instead of trembling at the message, as he might well have done, he assaulted him that brought it, in defiance of the wrath of which he was warned and contempt of that grace which sent him the warning. <hi type="italic">Rebuke a sinner</hi> and <hi type="italic">he will hate thee,</hi> and do thee a mischief if he can; yet God's prophets must rather expose themselves than betray their trust: he that employs them will protect them, and restrain the wrath of man, as he did Jeroboam's here by withering his hand, so that he could neither hurt the prophet nor draw it in to help himself. When his hand was stretched out to burn incense to his calves it was not withered; but, when it is stretched out against a prophet, he shall have no use of it till he humble himself. If God, in justice, harden the hearts of sinners, so that the hand they have stretched out in sin they cannot pull in again by repentance, that is a spiritual judgment, represented by this, and much more dreadful. <div eID="gen6795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6796" type="x-p"/> V. That word of God which should have touched his conscience humbled him not, but this which <hi type="italic">touched his bone and his flesh</hi> brings down his proud spirit. He looks for help now, 1. Not from his calves, but from God only, from his power and his favour. He wounded, and no hand but his can make whole. 2. When the prophet thus honoured God, by showing himself of a forgiving spirit, God put this further honour upon him, that at his word he recalled the judgment and by another miracle healed the withered hand, that by the goodness of God Jeroboam might be led to repentance, and, if he were not broken by the judgment, yet might be melted by the mercy. Not from his calves, but from God only, from his power and his favour. He wounded, and no hand but his can make whole. 2. But observe, He did not desire the prophet to pray that his sin might be pardoned, and his heart changed, only that his hand might be restored; thus Pharaoh would have Moses to pray that God would take away this death only (Exod. x. 17), not this sin. The prophet, as became a man of God, renders good for evil, upbraids not Jeroboam with his impotent malice, nor triumphs in his submission, but immediately addresses himself to God for him. Those only are entitled to the blessing Christ pronounced on the persecuted that learn of him to pray for their persecutors, Matt. v. 10, 44. When the prophet thus honoured God, by showing himself of a forgiving spirit, God put this further honour upon him, that at his word he recalled the judgment and by another miracle healed the withered hand, that by the goodness of God Jeroboam might be led to repentance, and, if he were not broken by the judgment, yet might be melted by the mercy. With both he seemed affected for the present, but the impressions wore off. VI. The prophet's refusal of Jeroboam's kind invitation, in which observe, 1. That God forbade his messenger to eat or drink in Beth-el (v. 9), to show his detestation of their execrable idolatry and apostasy from God, and to teach us not to have fellowship with the works of darkness, lest we have infection from them or give encouragement to them. He must not turn back the same way, but deliver his message, as it were, in transitu—as he passes along. He shall not seem to be sent on purpose (they were unworthy such a favour), but as if he only called by the way, his spirit being stirred, like Paul's at Athens, as he passed and saw their devotions. God would, by this command, try his prophet, as he did Ezekiel, whether he would not be rebellious, like that rebellious house, Ezek. ii. 8. 2. That the prophet, though hungry and weary, and perhaps poor, in obedience to the divine command refused both the entertainment and the reward proffered him. The obstinacy of Jeroboam in his idolatry (v. 33): He returned not from his evil way; some hand was found that durst repair the altar God had rent, and then Jeroboam offered sacrifice on it again, and the more boldly because the prophet who disturbed him before was in his grave (Rev. xi. 10) and because the prophecy was for a great while to come. Various methods had been used to reclaim him, but neither threats nor signs, neither judgments nor mercies, wrought upon him, so strangely was he wedded to his calves. He did not reform, no, not his priesthood, but whoever would, he filled his hand, and made him priest, though ever so illiterate or immoral, and of what tribe soever; and this became sin, that is, a snare first, and then a ruin, to Jeroboam's house, to cut if off, v. 34. Note, The diminution, disquiet, and desolation of families, are the fruit of sin; he promised himself that the calves would secure the crown to his family, but it proved they lost it, and sunk his family. Those betray themselves that think by any sin to support themselves.
